transcript:
Meeting header:
Date: 2026-02-03
Start time: 16:05 PST
Duration: 58 minutes
Attendees: Maya (Redwood AE), Jonah (Redwood SE), Carlos (Redwood SE), Priya (Cobalt ML), Liam (Cobalt Platform), Hana (Cobalt SRE)

Auto-summary (auto-generated, may be imperfect): Discussed POC scope for integrating Cobalt's client-side driver into Redwood's benchmark harness, clarified throughput and latency success criteria, looked at streaming tradeoffs, agreed on next steps to exchange scripts and run a two-day benchmark window.

[00:00] Maya: Hey everyone, thanks for carving out time. Quick roll call?
[00:08] Priya: Hi, Priya here.
[00:10] Liam: Liam, hi.
[00:12] Hana: Hana on my side.
[00:14] Jonah: Jonah here. Carlos also on.
[00:17] Carlos: Hey all.
[00:20] Maya: Cool. Goal for the hour is to scope the POC: specifically how your client-driver integrates with our harness, what success looks like — throughput, latency SLOs — and the timeline for a short benchmark run.

[00:35] Priya: Great. We want to validate our real traffic shapes. We're running a mix of short Q&A and longer generation tasks; roughly 70% short (<= 128 tokens), 30% long (400-1,200 tokens). Target is to prove 1,000 sustained QPS for short path and 120 concurrent long-gen sessions.

[01:03] Jonah: Couple clarifying q's: when you say 1,000 QPS, is that single-token requests or full request-per-call? Also are you streaming tokens back to the client for the long ones?

[01:18] Priya: It's requests per second, so end-to-end calls. For long gens we do streaming in prod — clients display tokens as they arrive.

[01:28] Liam: Important: cost is a top constraint. We're looking for tradeoffs that keep average token cost down; quantized models okay if quality holds.

[01:40] Maya: Understood. On cost/quality we can propose a quantized variant for dedicated nodes and fall back to a bfloat model for edge cases. But for the benchmark we should test both to quantify delta.

[02:02] Hana: Security note: the benchmark needs to run in a staging VPC peered with our network, because we run internal secrets for the client-driver that can't leave our VPC.

[02:15] Carlos: We've done ephemeral private nodes before; Redwood Private can be spun into a peered staging VPC and we can KMS-handle the keys. We'll need your peering CIDRs and a limited set of IPs for the harness controller.

[02:34] Priya: We'll provide that. Next: the client-driver is an async Python driver that maintains a small session cache client-side — it does its own retry/backoff. We'd like to plug that directly into your harness rather than reimplementing logic server-side.

[02:52] Jonah: That's ideal. We'll build an adapter so your driver talks to the harness controller over the standard driver API. It'll accept a mapping file: which endpoints to call, session lifetimes, concurrency envelopes. We have a skeleton adapter in the repo.

[03:10] Priya: One risk: our client does streaming partials and occasionally patches previous tokens (edit-insert style). Does your runtime support streaming edits?

[03:22] Jonah: Streaming partials yes; edits in stream are trickier. For the POC we can emulate insert edits by re-sending a short amend call — but we should instrument them as a separate request type in the harness so we can track cost and latency.

[03:41] Liam: On metrics — we care about p50/p95/p99 latency per request type, token throughput, and token cost per 1k tokens. Also end-to-end time-to-first-token for streaming sessions.

[03:56] Maya: We'll surface all of that in the dashboards. The harness emits traces and token counters; we can wire them to your Datadog or export CSV.

[04:10] Hana: How do you handle warm starts? If we spin up a pool, cold-start variability could skew P99 badly.

[04:20] Carlos: Good point — we'll do a warmup pass to populate KV cache and JIT kernels as part of the benchmark. We typically run a 30-minute warmup at lower QPS then ramp to target.

[04:35] Priya: Can you describe the warmup script? We want to use representative prompts, not synthetic ones.

[04:42] Jonah: We recommend a 3-phase ramp: 1) priming using your 50 most common prompts to populate attention caches and vocabulary kernels, 2) concurrency ramp to target for 10 minutes, 3) sustained run for measurement. We'll provide the harness steps; you'll supply the prompt files.

[05:01] Liam: About streaming vs non-streaming — streaming lowers perceived latency but can increase overall cost and noise in p99 because of extra network round trips. We need quantifiable guidance: if streaming gives us 100ms TTF (time-to-first-token) improvement but 12% higher token cost, is it worth it?

[05:20] Maya: We'll benchmark both. We'll also measure token output delta for quantized vs fp16 to check quality regressions. If the quality holds within your thresholds (you define), we can recommend the cheaper path for most calls and stream for interactive long sessions.

[05:37] Priya: Our success criteria: 1) p95 <= 250ms for short requests (<=128 tokens), 2) sustained 1,000 RPS on short path for 30-minute window, 3) streaming long gens TTF <= 600ms, 4) token-cost delta <= 15% vs baseline. If those are met we move to a three-week pilot cluster.

[06:00] Maya: Sounds reasonable. We'll push targets into the benchmark harness so the output CSV flags pass/fail for each metric.

[06:12] Hana: Network egress: we need assurance of encryption in transit and that logs containing prompts are not persisted in long-term storage.

[06:22] Carlos: We can disable persistent storage for the run and stream logs to ephemeral S3 with 7-day retention, or use an in-memory sink for traces. KMS keys are scoped to your account on Private nodes.

[06:40] Priya: Cool. About the adapter: our driver handles adaptive concurrency — it will ramp up when latencies are good and back off on errors. Will the harness allow client-side adaptive behavior or does the harness control concurrency?

[06:56] Jonah: Adapter supports two modes: harness-driven concurrency (recommended to get steady-state numbers) and client-driven (to emulate prod behavior). For initial benchmark let's do harness-driven to reach target throughput, then a second run with your adaptive driver for realistic traffic patterns.

[07:18] Liam: For the realistic run we want to capture retry storms and how the runtime copes under backpressure.

[07:26] Maya: We'll include a failure-injection toggle (endpoint latency + packet loss emulation) in the harness to observe behavior.

[07:35] Priya: About model variants — we run a custom fine-tuned model. Is Redwood able to onboard a customer-compiled model or do we need to export to a specific format?

[07:49] Carlos: We support ONNX and some torchscript formats plus specific conversion for quantized kernels. We'll need a model artifact or build instructions. In the POC we can test with a close open model to measure baseline then swap in your fine-tuned artifact for a final run.

[08:10] Priya: We'll try to export a trimmed artifact. If not possible, we'll accept evaluation on proxy model for perf and then a final run with the actual binary in the Private staging environment.

[08:25] Jonah: Important note: sequence length distribution affects kernel choice. If you have lots of 1,200-token gens, kernel selection and memory tiling differ greatly than 128-token bursts. Please include token histogram.

[08:38] Priya: Will do. We'll attach per-endpoint token hist CSV.

[08:45] Liam: Also, can we capture per-token throughput and per-request cost in same CSV?

[08:52] Maya: Yes — harness outputs a combined trace per request with token_count, time-to-first-token, total-latency, and backend-cost-estimate. We can also add a flag to compute cost normalized to your pricing assumptions.

[09:08] Hana: How about the harness controller: is it open source? We were hoping to review the adapter code before the run.

[09:15] Jonah: The harness repo is public (link shared). The adapter skeleton will be a small PR you can review. We'll also give a runbook for the benchmark.

[09:25] Priya: Please include the specific Python version, asyncio lib versions, and any pinned deps — our driver is sensitive to minor differences.

[09:31] Carlos: We'll add an environment matrix in the README.

[09:37] Maya: Quick timeline proposal: adapter + runbook out by 2/5, customer scripts and token hist by 2/6, staging creds and peering by 2/8, warmup + benchmark window target 2/10-2/11, initial results deck by 2/12. Does that work?

[09:55] Priya: That's tight but doable. We may need to shift by a day if export takes longer, but we'll try.

[10:03] Liam: On hardware: what's the target node spec for the dedicated nodes? GPU types matter for quantization kernels.

[10:11] Carlos: For the initial runs we'll propose A100 80GB equiv for long gens and 1xH100-style for quantized load if available; we'll list exact SKUs in the runbook. We'll also show a cheaper config for cost comparisons (e.g., 8-bit quantized on 80GB Ampere).

[10:30] Priya: Do you have any tips to reduce p99 noise? We use warmed persistent workers in prod — is that recommended for the benchmark?

[10:38] Jonah: Yes, pinned workers with KV cache persistence reduce p99 variance. For the benchmark, we'll run both pinned and ephemeral modes and show the delta. Document both so you can pick a deployment option.

[10:53] Hana: Instrumentation: we need request IDs propagated so we can tie application logs to harness traces.

[10:59] Maya: We'll annotate every request with X-Request-ID and include it in the exported trace.

[11:06] Priya: One more operational ask: if the adaptive driver triggers a backoff cascade, can the harness throttle at the controller instead of killing connections? We want to observe graceful degradation.

[11:16] Jonah: Yes — we have a controller-level circuit-breaker that will queue or reject at configured thresholds. We'll surface those events.

[11:26] Liam: For reporting — we want a pass/fail summary and raw CSVs. Also an executive one-pager comparing cost/latency across tested model variants.

[11:36] Maya: We'll provide both a detailed artifact and a 1-pager.

[11:42] Priya: What about shared artifacts? Please share links in the follow-up.

[11:45] Maya: We'll attach the harness repo, the adapter skeleton, the runbook, and a sample result deck.

[11:52] Hana: Access control wise, ensure the results deck redacts prompts unless we explicitly allow them.

[11:58] Carlos: Noted; by default we'll mask prompt text and only show token length and anonymized text.

[12:05] Maya: Recap and next steps: we've written the action items in the chat — Maya will send calendar invites for the benchmark window, Jonah will share adapter skeleton by 2/5, Priya will upload scripts by 2/6, Hana will provide peering details by 2/7. We'll aim to run on 2/10 or 2/11 with a warmup then steady-state run.

[12:30] Priya: Thanks everyone.
[12:33] Liam: Thanks.
[12:34] Maya: Thanks, bye.
